**fable-graph review of head 8d49c37c0235aeda38be368576685219c8232472 (unarmed; one commit, three files): APPROVED.**

Read: `Collector.list_runs` keeps the first page's `total_count` as the floor for each day's listing (runs created while pages are read only add to it), counts DISTINCT run ids after the page loop, and raises `ListingShort` naming the event, day, listed/total and the page reached (with "(the 10-page cap)" when that was the cause) when the count is missing or the listing is short; a short day is asked once more, and a listing that is still short propagates; a short listing is never cached (`_cached` only stores a successful fetch). The CLI catches `ListingShort`, prints `collect: LISTING SHORT: …; the corpus is not rewritten: every pair needing a missing run would have been dropped` and exits 1, so the corpus is never silently built from a partial listing, which is exactly the 256-vs-304 pairing drop the read-back could not explain.

Verified on a scratch worktree of this head (python3.13 `-B`, purged `__pycache__`): `test_reuse_policy_replay.py` Ran 114 OK. Break-confirms, each shown as the applied diff and restored through git: the guard removed fails five tests (short-then-fail, repeated run, missing count, short-then-whole, truncated later page); rows counted instead of distinct ids fails the repeated-run test; a missing `total_count` accepted fails the no-total test; the second ask removed fails the short-then-whole test. The live control (the guarded listing from 09-24 to now reading 1416 pull_request and 846 merge_group runs with no shortfall) is the right positive control: the guard passes real data and fails the planted shortfalls.

One thing for the next collect run's body, not a condition: when the guard first fires in the wild, record the day, event and listed/total in the design note's instrument log; a count of how often GitHub's paging comes back short is itself the measurement this guard makes possible.
